text.text: The studio desk for an interior designer: each project from discovery to install, every piece you specify and order with trade and client prices, the approvals that unlock each phase, and the fee invoices that keep the studio paid.

This workspace is the studio's desk: who the clients are, what phase each project is in, every piece specified and ordered, what the client still has to approve, and which fee invoices are out. Your accounting software keeps the books; this is where the design work is run.

text.text: The Ebbesen dining pendant arrived damaged, so the procurement assistant files the claim with the vendor and moves the install back one week. The purchasing deposit invoice is overdue, so nothing else is ordered for that project until it is paid.

Every project moves through the same phases. Each one ends with a client approval, and the next one does not start until that approval is in. That rule protects your time and keeps fees tied to finished work.

cells.text: Site visit, measurements, photos, budget and wish list
Signed letter of agreement and retainer paid

Present it in person or on a call; never by email alone for the first presentation.

Your letter of agreement should say how many revision rounds each phase includes. When a client asks for a fourth concept, show them the agreement kindly and offer the extra round at your hourly rate. Record that conversation on the approval.
on the project shows how many decisions are open.
Approvals past their date appear in the overdue view. Call, do not email.
A project waiting more than two weeks on a decision gets a check-in about timing and budget, not just the decision.

The Obuya-Hartley floor plan came back with changes: the bed on the long wall and a reading chair by the window. The second concept round is due this week; material selections follow once the plan is approved.
Talk money in every phase, not just procurement. A client who saw a clear budget at concept is rarely surprised by the proposal.
Procurement is where studios earn a large share of their income and lose most of their time. Every piece is tracked from the moment it is specified until it is installed.

The built-in bookcase panels for the Marchetti office were expected three days ago. The assistant calls the millwork shop, learns they ship this week, updates the date and lets the client know the install moves two days.
Design fees pay for the studio's time. Bill them on a schedule tied to the phases, so you are never far ahead of what the client has paid.

text.text: on each project adds sent and overdue invoices.
Log time weekly, even when you bill monthly. Send the client a short summary with each invoice: hours by phase and what was done. Clients who see the work rarely question the bill.
Do not pay a vendor deposit with studio money before the client's purchasing deposit has cleared. If a client stops paying, you are left holding furniture made to their taste.

The Ebbesen purchasing deposit is ten days overdue. The lead designer calls, learns the client was travelling, and agrees payment by Friday. The walnut table already shipped against an earlier deposit, so nothing new is ordered until then.
Installation is the day clients remember. Plan it like an event: everything received and inspected, a timed plan, and the room finished and styled before the client walks in.
